claims.text: Toughness retention in high-entropy alloys largely depends on the stability and distribution of nanoscale precipitates at grain boundaries.
A controlled heat treatment can induce precipitate coarsening without changing the alloy's overall composition.
Heat-induced precipitate coarsening degrades grain-boundary cohesion.
Heat-induced precipitate coarsening weakens crack-deflection mechanisms.
Heat-induced precipitate coarsening weakens crack-bridging mechanisms.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion and weakened crack deflection and bridging diminish fracture energy absorption.
Diminished energy absorption during fracture reduces toughness.
Samples with coarsened precipitates will have significantly lower toughness than untreated samples with fine precipitates.
The magnitude of toughness loss will correlate with the degree of precipitate coarsening.
A fine, uniformly distributed nanoscale precipitate population provides high toughness in the baseline alloy.
The proposed behavior applies to high-entropy alloys in which nanoscale precipitates are the primary toughening mechanism.
The proposed behavior applies under quasi-static loading at room temperature.
The precipitate-coarsening threshold for toughness decline may vary among high-entropy-alloy systems.

contradictions.description: The alloy is described as homogeneous and single-phase while also containing a distribution of nanoscale precipitates. Distinct precipitates normally constitute an additional phase, so the phase-state terminology is internally inconsistent unless the precipitates are explicitly defined as same-phase features.
The stated scope is quasi-static loading, but Charpy impact energy is proposed as an outcome and falsification measurement; an impact test is dynamic rather than quasi-static.
